blocks.text: "In the early hours of a very cold harmattan morning" is twelve words long. "He ran" is two. Yet the long group is only a phrase and the short one is a full clause. Length has nothing to do with it — and once you know what does, a whole family of exam questions becomes routine.

blocks.title: Phrase
blocks.text: A group of words that works as a single unit in a sentence but contains no subject together with a finite verb. Because it has no finite verb, a phrase can never stand alone as a sentence.

blocks.markdown:
### The one test that matters

Look for a **subject plus a finite verb**. A finite verb shows tense and agrees with a subject: *runs*, *ran*, *was running*, *has run*.

- *at the beginning of the harmattan* — no subject, no finite verb → **phrase**
- *when the harmattan begins* — subject *the harmattan*, finite verb *begins* → **clause**

Non-finite verb forms do not count. Participles (*racing*, *finished*), gerunds (*swimming*) and infinitives (*to study*) show no tense and take no subject, so a group built on them is still a phrase.

### Form and function are two different questions

Examiners ask both, so keep them apart in your mind.

**Form** describes how the phrase is built: prepositional, participial, gerund, infinitive, noun, verb.

**Function** describes the job it does in the sentence: nominal (like a noun), adjectival (describing a noun) or adverbial (modifying a verb).

One phrase can be prepositional in form and adjectival in function at the same time — *the boy **with the red cap*** is exactly that.

rows: The boy **with the red cap** won.
She travelled to Ibadan **to study medicine**.
blocks.caption: Deciding a phrase's function by the question it answers

blocks.title: Analysing every phrase in a sentence
blocks.prompt: State the form and function of each phrase in: "Racing down the slope, the boy in the blue shirt lost control of his bicycle."

steps.text: Find the finite verb of the sentence: *lost*. Everything else is built around it.
Take *Racing down the slope*. It is built on the participle *racing*, so its form is participial. It tells us what the boy was doing, so it describes the noun *boy* — function: adjectival.
Take *in the blue shirt*. It begins with the preposition *in*, so its form is prepositional. It tells us which boy — function: adjectival.
Take *of his bicycle*. Prepositional in form again. It completes the noun *control*, telling us control of what — function: adjectival, completing the noun phrase *control of his bicycle*.
Confirm that none of the three has a subject with a finite verb, so all three are phrases rather than clauses.

blocks.answer: Racing down the slope = participial phrase, adjectival; in the blue shirt = prepositional phrase, adjectival; of his bicycle = prepositional phrase, adjectival

items: A **noun phrase** is the head noun plus everything modifying it: *the tall boy in the blue shirt*.
A **verb phrase** is the main verb plus its auxiliaries: *has been repairing*.
A **prepositional phrase** starts with a preposition and ends with its object: *under the mango tree*.
A **participial phrase** starts with a present or past participle: *racing down the slope*, *worn out by the journey*.
A **gerund phrase** is an -ing phrase doing a noun's job: *swimming in the lagoon*.
An **infinitive phrase** starts with *to* plus a verb: *to study medicine at Ibadan*.

blocks.title: Substitution proves the boundary
blocks.text: To find where a noun phrase ends, replace the whole group with a single pronoun. In "The tall boy in the blue shirt is my cousin", *He is my cousin* works, so the entire group *The tall boy in the blue shirt* is one noun phrase, not just *the tall boy*.

blocks.title: WAEC and NECO tip
blocks.text: When a question underlines a group of words and asks what it is, answer in two moves: first check for a subject and finite verb to settle phrase or clause, then ask which question the group answers — who/what, which one, or when/where/how/why — to settle its function.

points: A phrase is a word group with no subject and finite verb, so it can never stand alone.
Participles, gerunds and infinitives are non-finite, so groups built on them remain phrases.
Form tells you how a phrase is built; function tells you what job it does.
A phrase functions nominally, adjectivally or adverbially, and the question it answers reveals which.
Replace a group with one pronoun to test where a noun phrase begins and ends.
